'''''Allium nigrum''''', common name '''black garlic''', '''broad-leaved leek''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''broadleaf garlic''', is a [[Middle Eastern]] species of [[wild onion]]. It lacks the onion or garlic scent shared by most of the other species in the group. The species is native to [[Turkey]], [[Cyprus]], [[Syria]], [[Lebanon]], and the [[Palestine (region)|Palestine region]] but cultivated as an ornamental in many other places.<ref name=wclnigrum/> It has become naturalized in some regions, including parts of the [[United States]] (especially [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Oregon]]).<ref name="asdfjkh892475y038h45tenrgio39046">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101380 Flora of North America v 26 p 243, ''Allium nigrum'']</ref><ref name="Bailey, L.H. 1976">Bailey, L.H. & E.Z. Bailey. 1976. Hortus Third i–xiv, 1–1290. MacMillan, New York.</ref>

== Description ==

''Allium nigrum'' produces asymmetric bulbs up to 5 cm across. Each plant has 3-6 leaves, lanceolate in shape, flat and bent to the side, up to 60 cm long and 2.5 cm across. Later the leaves become reflexed. [[Scape (botany)|Scapes]] are smooth and round in cross-section, 80–100 cm tall. The scape carries a dense umbellate inflorescence with star-like flowers up to 9 mm across; the [[tepals]] are white with a green midvein; the [[anthers]] are purple or yellow. The [[ovary (botany)|ovaries]] are black-green (but flushed with red in the [[Levant]]) in [[anthesis]], but green when younger or following anthesis.<ref name="asdfjkh892475y038h45tenrgio39046"/><ref name="Bailey, L.H. 1976"/><ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11628884#page/446/mode/1up Linnaeus, Carl von. 1762. Species Plantarum, Editio Secunda 1: 430.]</ref><ref>Hitchcock, C. H., A.J. Cronquist, F. M. Ownbey & J. W. Thompson. 1969. Vascular Cryptogams, Gymnosperms, and Monocotyledons. 1: 1–914. In C. L. Hitchcock, Vascular Plants of the Pacific Northwest. University of Washington Press, Seattle.</ref>{{sfn|Fritsch et al|2006}}

== Taxonomy ==
It is the [[type species]] of [[Subgenus]] (Section) ''Melanocrommyum''. Molecular evidence suggests that ''A. nigrum'' is a [[polymorphism (biology)|polymorphous]] species consisting of several [[infraspecific]] groups.{{sfn|Fragman-Sapir|Fritsch|2011}}

=== Subdivision ===
Alliances:{{sfn|Fragman-Sapir|Fritsch|2011}}
* ''Allium nigrum''
* ''Allium asclepiadeum''
* ''Allium orientale''

'''''Allium nigrum alliance''''':
''Allium nigrum'' [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] and ''A. multibulbosum'' [[Jacq.]] have often been treated as [[variety (botany)|variants]] within a variable ''A. nigrum'' ''[[sensu lato]]''. The type variant, ''A. nigrum'' ''[[sensu stricto]]'' is characterised by rose oblong tepals, rose filaments, and distinctly tri-sulcate, strongly coarse, dull, permanently green ovaries, while ''A. multibulbosum'' have white to pinkish-carmine, oblong tepals, filaments of the same color as tepals, but rounded, narrowly hexasulcate, smooth and commonly glossy ovaries. The latter commonly turn green from black, but some are permanently green. These variants are in a [[sister group]] relationship. The [[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] (WCLSPF) treat these as separate species.<ref name=wclnigrum/><ref name=wclmulti/>

However, ''[[Allium basalticum]]'' has been considered sufficiently distinct on [[molecular phylogenetics|molecular grounds]], to be recognised as a new separate species.<ref name=wclbasalt/> Another distinct species is ''[[Allium dumetorum]]''.<ref name=wcldumet/>{{sfn|Fragman-Sapir|Fritsch|2011}}

'''''Allium asclepiadeum alliance''''':
''[[Allium asclepiadeum]]'' [[Bornm.]] was initially considered a separate species, but then submerged in ''A. nigrum''. It has again been treated as a separate species based on molecular data, but under the new name of ''[[Allium meronense]]'' Fragman & R.M. Fritsch. WCLSPF, while accepting this new species,<ref name=wclmeron/> have retained ''A. asclepiadeum'' as a separate species.<ref name=wclbasclep/>{{sfn|Fragman-Sapir|Fritsch|2011}}

'''''Allium orientale alliance''''': descriptions of ''[[Allium orientale]]'' [[Boiss.]] have varied, resulting in the name being applied to a variety of different plants, a concept not supported by molecular data which indicate ''[[Allium israeliticum]]'' Fragman & R.M. Fritsch, as a distinct new species. WCLSPF recognises both as distinct species.<ref name=wclorient/><ref name=wclisrael/>{{sfn|Fragman-Sapir|Fritsch|2011}}

=== Etymology ===
The name ''nigrum'' ([[Latin]]: black) is derived from the colour of the ovaries.{{sfn|Fritsch et al|2006}}

==Uses==
The plant is a frequent ornamental in European and North American gardens, having been introduced in the early twentieth century.{{sfn|Fritsch et al|2006}} It is produced in [[Taean County|Taean]] and [[Seosan]] in South Korea.
